summary: Defines two authentication protocols for PPP, the Password Authentication Protocol and the Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol. It was replaced by RFC 1994.

eli5.summary: Before letting someone in, you check who they are. PAP just asks for a password, while CHAP asks a trick question that only the right person can answer.

subtitle: Two methods to verify that the other end of a PPP link is who it claims to be.

tldr.problem: When two systems connect over PPP, they need to authenticate each other before exchanging user data. Different situations call for different security levels.
tldr.mechanism: PPP offers two authentication protocols: PAP uses a password sent plainly, and CHAP asks a cryptographic challenge that only the right peer can answer correctly.
tldr.outcome: Authentication happens during the PPP Link Establishment phase before any network-layer protocols run. CHAP is stronger and should be preferred.

facts.label: CHAP secret minimum size
facts.value: 1 octet; at least 16 octets recommended for MD5

today: RFC 1334 was replaced by RFC 1994, which updates these protocols and is now the standard definition. The authentication mechanisms defined here are historical; implementations should follow the newer RFC.

sections.title: How PPP Connects Two Systems
sections.content:
The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) is the standard way dial-up connections and similar links work. PPP has three phases: first, the Link Establishment phase sets up the connection itself using the Link Control Protocol. Second, the Authentication phase lets each end verify the other. Third, the Network-Layer Protocol phase sends actual data. This RFC defines the authentication part.

By default, authentication is optional. If authentication is wanted, each end declares which authentication protocol to use during Link Establishment. The authenticator (the end demanding proof) specifies the protocol; the peer (the end being authenticated) must answer.
sections.eli5: PPP is how dial-up works. First both sides say hello and agree on what to do. Then they prove who they are. Then they can talk to each other.

sections.title: Password Authentication Protocol (PAP)
sections.content:
The Password Authentication Protocol (PAP) is simple: the peer sends a plaintext user ID and password, and the authenticator checks if they match. The peer can retry after a rejection, and by default the authenticator should accept repeated attempts until either the connection succeeds or a timeout expires.

PAP is weak: passwords travel in the clear, so anyone listening can read them. Replay attacks are possible—an attacker can capture a valid message and send it again later. The RFC warns that PAP should only be used where a plaintext password was already needed, such as simulating a login to a remote host. Implementations that support CHAP MUST offer CHAP before offering PAP.
sections.eli5: PAP is like saying your password out loud. Anyone listening can hear it. It is simple but not safe.

sections.title: PAP and CHAP Message Formats
sections.content:
Both protocols wrap their messages in a simple packet: a 1-byte Code field identifies the packet type, a 1-byte Identifier helps match requests to replies, and a 2-byte Length field tells the packet size. The Data field varies by packet type.

In PAP, the peer sends Code 1 (Authenticate-Request) with a peer ID and password. The authenticator replies with Code 2 (Authenticate-Ack) on success or Code 3 (Authenticate-Nak) on failure. In CHAP, the authenticator sends Code 1 (Challenge); the peer responds with Code 2 (Response); the authenticator then sends Code 3 (Success) or Code 4 (Failure). Both use the same encapsulation.
sections.eli5: Messages are small packets with a type tag, an ID number to track them, and the data.

sections.title: Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol (CHAP)
sections.content:
CHAP is stronger than PAP. The Challenge-Handshake Authentication Protocol uses a three-message exchange. The authenticator sends a random challenge value. The peer computes a one-way hash of the challenge mixed with a secret (usually using MD5) and sends the hash back. The authenticator compares it to its own calculation. If they match, the peer is verified. If not, the connection closes.

The secret is never sent over the network, only the hash of it combined with the challenge. Since each challenge is different, CHAP resists replay attacks: a captured response cannot be reused because the next challenge will be different. CHAP can even periodically re-challenge the peer during an established connection to ensure the connection has not been hijacked.
sections.eli5: CHAP asks a question where the right answer depends on a secret. Only the person who knows the secret can answer. And the question is different each time.

sections.title: Security Issues and Best Practices
sections.content:
Authentication happens at different times and using different protocols in each direction, and no rule requires the same secret to be used in both. Implementations should store secrets carefully, limiting access to the authentication process only. When distributing secrets, use minimal handling—ideally only the authentication subsystem ever sees them.

Re-tries of failed authentication should not reset failure counters until after a successful authentication or an explicit link termination. The implementation should offer CHAP to all users by default; if PAP is needed at all, it should be a conscious choice per user, not a default. Some implementations use the transaction ID in the message header to detect retransmitted requests and avoid re-authenticating a user who has already succeeded.
sections.eli5: Keep secrets safe. Use the same secret only for one user so an attacker cannot trick the system into accepting the weakest password. CHAP is better than PAP.
